worksheet.title: Which One Is Wrong?
worksheet.subtitle: One script misses the goal — find it
worksheet.learning_goal: I can compare two scripts to a goal and find which one has a bug.

parts.title: The goal: meet on 3
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) both start on the green flag. They are SUPPOSED to MEET on number 3. But one of the two scripts has a bug, so it does not reach 3. Read both scripts, run them, and figure out WHICH sprite's script is wrong.

parts.title: Run both
parts.prompt: Where does each land? Bit (home 0, forward 3): ____  Pixel (home 5, back 1): ____. Do BOTH reach the goal 3?

parts.title: Which one is wrong?
parts.prompt: Which sprite's script is WRONG — Bit's or Pixel's? Write it. How do you know? (Hint: one sprite already reaches 3.)

parts.title: How far off?
parts.prompt: The goal is 3. The wrong sprite landed on ____. That is ____ number(s) away from the goal.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To find a bug in two scripts, compare each one to the GOAL. The script that already reaches the goal is correct. The one that misses is the buggy one — and that tells you where to look.

teacher_guide.title: Which One Is Wrong?
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 2. Which One Is Wrong? — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students learn the core debugging move for two parallel scripts: compare EACH script to the goal to locate the bug. Here the goal is 'meet on 3'; Bit reaches it and Pixel does not, so Pixel's script is the buggy one. Diagnosing which of two concurrent scripts is wrong (before fixing) is the Grade-2 C3.2 reading-and-locating skill the rest of the subject builds on.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a star marker on square 3 (the goal) and two counters; run both and see which counter misses the star.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: state the goal — 'both should meet on 3.' Run Bit: 0 forward 3 → 3 (on the star).
2. WE DO: run Pixel: 5 back 1 → 4 (misses the star). 'Since Bit is right, the bug is in Pixel.'
3. YOU DO: students name Pixel as the wrong script and say it is 1 away from the goal.
4. Connect: 'Compare each script to the goal — the one that misses is the bug.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Bit: 0 → forward 3 → 3. Pixel: 5 → back 1 → 4. Bit reaches the goal 3; Pixel does NOT (so not both reach it).
Ex 2 — Pixel's script is wrong. We know because Bit already lands on the goal 3, so the bug must be in the other script.
Ex 3 — the goal is 3; the wrong sprite (Pixel) landed on 4, which is 1 number away from the goal.
Diagnosis note: this sheet only LOCATES the bug; fixing specific bug types comes on the next sheets.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: assuming the bug is in Bit because Pixel 'looks fine' — always check each against the goal number.
Common error: trying to fix before locating — this sheet is about WHICH script is wrong, not the fix yet.
Simplify: mark the goal square, run each sprite, and circle the one that does not land on it.
Extend: ask what single move would fix Pixel (back 2 instead of back 1) — a preview of the next sheets.
Success indicator: the child names Pixel as the buggy script and says it is 1 away from the goal.
